title: Architecture in Agile and DevOps Environments
objectives: Practice architecture that enables agile delivery without sacrificing quality
Apply just-enough-up-front design for government services
Embed architecture decisions within sprint cycles rather than before them
Use architecture runway to stay ahead of delivery without blocking it
Balance emergent design with intentional architecture in regulated environments
whyThisMatters:
The GDS Service Manual prescribes agile delivery for government digital services. Discovery, alpha, beta, live — this is the delivery framework within which architects must work. Yet architecture is often perceived as anti-agile: big up-front design, heavyweight documentation, governance gates that slow delivery.

This perception is wrong but understandable. Traditional architecture practice — producing comprehensive design documents before development begins, requiring sign-off before any code is written — does not fit agile delivery. But the answer is not to abandon architecture. The answer is to practice architecture differently: lighter, faster, more collaborative, and more embedded in delivery.

In government, the tension is real. Agile delivery wants to move fast and respond to learning. Government governance wants assurance, accountability, and documentation. Security teams want threat models before code is written. Service assessments want evidence of good decision-making. The architect's role is to satisfy both — enabling fast delivery while maintaining the quality, security, and strategic alignment that government requires. This is possible, but it requires a different way of working from either traditional architecture or pure agile.

content.heading: The False Dichotomy: Architecture vs Agile
content.body:
The idea that architecture and agile are incompatible rests on a misunderstanding of both. Traditional architecture (comprehensive design before any code) is indeed incompatible with agile. But architecture itself — making good structural decisions — is essential in any delivery model.

Agile does not mean 'no design.' It means 'enough design at the right time.' The question changes from 'have we designed everything before we start?' to 'have we designed enough to start, and will we continue designing as we learn?'

In government agile delivery, architecture decisions fall into three categories:

Decisions that must be made early because they are expensive to reverse: hosting platform, primary technology stack, authentication approach, data classification and security boundaries, integration patterns with existing systems. These are your 'just enough up-front design' — the architectural foundations that the team needs before they can build anything.

Decisions that should be deferred until you have more information: detailed data models (evolve as you understand the domain), specific component designs (emerge from implementation), performance optimisation (respond to actual usage patterns), and technology choices for non-critical components (decide when you reach them).

Decisions that emerge from delivery: detailed API contracts (evolve through integration testing), error handling patterns (emerge from real failure modes), caching strategies (respond to actual performance data), and user journey optimisations (respond to user research findings).

The skill is knowing which category each decision belongs to. Making a deferrable decision too early wastes effort and may be wrong. Deferring a foundational decision too long creates expensive rework. The GDS delivery phases provide natural decision points: discovery identifies constraints and high-level options, alpha validates the technical approach through prototyping, beta makes remaining decisions through iterative delivery.

content.heading: Just-Enough Up-Front Design
content.body:
Just-enough up-front design means making the minimum set of architectural decisions needed for a team to begin delivery with confidence, while deferring everything that can wait until more information is available.

For a typical government service entering alpha, 'just enough' includes:

Hosting and infrastructure decisions: where will this run? Which cloud provider (or on-premise)? Which region? This is needed early because it affects everything else — security, compliance, cost, and available services.

Security architecture: what is the data classification? What security boundaries exist? What authentication and authorisation approach will be used? These are needed early because retrofitting security is expensive and dangerous.

Integration architecture: what existing systems must this service interact with? What are their interfaces? What are the constraints on data exchange? These are needed early because they shape the service's boundary and determine dependencies.

Key technology choices: what programming language, what framework, what database technology? These are needed early because they determine what skills the team needs and what patterns are available.

Non-functional requirements: what performance, availability, and scalability are expected? These are needed early because they influence fundamental architectural patterns (synchronous vs asynchronous, single-region vs multi-region).

What is explicitly NOT needed up-front: detailed data models (they will evolve), detailed component designs (they will emerge), specific library choices (the team decides during delivery), UI architecture (evolves with user research), and operational tooling choices (decided as operational needs become clear).

Document the up-front decisions as ADRs. Keep them concise. Make them available to the team. Then get out of the way and let delivery begin.

content.heading: The Architecture Runway
content.body:
The architecture runway is a concept from Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe) that applies well to government delivery. It means maintaining a small amount of prepared architecture ahead of what the team is currently building — enough to keep delivery moving without blocking on architectural decisions, but not so much that you are designing far ahead of implementation.

Think of it like a motorway being built: you do not need to design the entire route before construction begins, but you do need the next section designed before the construction crew reaches it. If construction catches up to design, the crew has to stop and wait. If design races too far ahead, conditions may change and the design may need revision.

In practice, the architecture runway means:

The architect works one or two sprints ahead of the delivery team on architectural concerns. While the team builds sprint N's features, the architect is resolving the architectural questions that sprint N+1 or N+2 will encounter. This might mean: investigating an integration option, writing an ADR for a technology choice, producing a sequence diagram for a complex interaction, or resolving a security question with the security team.

Runway items are identified through backlog review. The architect regularly reviews the upcoming backlog and identifies items with architectural implications. These are flagged, and the architectural investigation happens before the team picks up the work — so when they reach it, the architectural direction is clear.

Runway is not detailed design. It is answering the questions that would block the team if unanswered. 'Should we use synchronous or asynchronous processing for this workflow?' is a runway question. 'What should the exact JSON schema of this API response look like?' is a detail that the team can resolve during implementation.

The runway collapses in two situations: when the architect is too busy with other work to stay ahead, and when unexpected technical discoveries create questions nobody anticipated. Both are normal — the response is to slow delivery briefly while the architectural question is resolved, rather than allowing the team to proceed in a direction that may be wrong.

content.heading: The Architect's Role in Sprint Ceremonies
content.body:
In agile government teams, the architect is embedded in the delivery team — not a separate function that reviews from outside. Embedding means participating in sprint ceremonies and making architecture a continuous activity rather than a phase.

Sprint Planning: the architect participates to identify stories with architectural implications, ensure the team understands the architectural direction for their work, and flag items that need runway investigation before they can be picked up. The architect does not plan the sprint (that is the team's responsibility) but ensures architectural concerns are visible.

Daily Stand-up: brief attendance (or asynchronous update) to stay aware of what the team is building and whether any unexpected architectural questions have emerged. The architect does not need to attend every stand-up — but they need to be accessible when the team encounters architectural decisions they cannot make themselves.

Refinement: the architect's most important ceremony. During backlog refinement, the architect helps the team understand the architectural implications of upcoming stories, identifies dependencies, and answers technical questions. This is where runway preparation happens — the architect raises questions that need resolution before the story can be built.

Retrospective: the architect participates to understand how architecture processes are affecting the team. Are architectural decisions causing delays? Are ADRs useful or burdensome? Is the design authority adding value or slowing things down? The architect adapts their practices based on team feedback.

Demo/Review: the architect observes what has been built and checks alignment with the architectural direction. If the implementation has drifted from the intended architecture, this is the time to catch it — before it compounds further. But the response should be coaching, not criticism: 'I notice the data layer is tightly coupled to the API — was that a deliberate decision? Let me explain why loose coupling would help us here.'

The key principle: the architect serves the team, not the other way around. Architecture enables delivery — it does not govern it. When the architect is experienced as helpful (resolving blockers, providing clarity, improving quality), teams engage willingly. When architecture is experienced as bureaucracy (blocking progress, requiring documentation, imposing decisions), teams resist.

content.heading: Balancing Emergent Design with Intentional Architecture
content.body:
Pure emergent design — letting the architecture evolve entirely from implementation decisions — works for simple systems but fails for government services that must integrate with existing systems, meet security requirements, support multiple channels, and survive for years.

Pure intentional architecture — designing everything up-front before any code is written — works for stable, well-understood problems but fails when requirements evolve, users behave unexpectedly, and technologies change during delivery.

Government services need both. Intentional architecture provides the structural foundations that keep the system coherent as it grows. Emergent design fills in the details as the team learns about the problem and the solution.

What should be intentional: system boundaries and integration points (these affect other teams and systems), security architecture (cannot be retrofitted safely), data ownership and privacy boundaries (legal compliance requirements), deployment architecture and operational model (affects the operations team), and standards compliance (TCoP, accessibility, API standards).

What should emerge: internal component structure (evolves with understanding), specific data models (evolve with domain knowledge), performance optimisations (respond to real usage data), error handling patterns (emerge from real failure modes), and user interface architecture (evolves with user research).

The practical balance: architect the boundaries, let the internals emerge. Define how the system interacts with the outside world (APIs, integrations, security boundaries, data flows). Let the team decide how to implement the internals — they are closest to the problem and will make better detailed decisions than an architect working at a distance.

This balance also maps to documentation: intentional architecture is documented (solution architecture document, ADRs, security architecture). Emergent design lives in the code (self-documenting through good naming, clear structure, and automated tests). Not everything needs a document — but the structural decisions do.

content.heading: Architecture Through Government Delivery Phases
content.body:
The GDS delivery phases (discovery, alpha, beta, live) provide natural checkpoints for architectural maturity.

Discovery: Architecture is exploratory. The architect identifies constraints, assesses existing systems that must be integrated, understands security and data protection requirements, and forms initial hypotheses about the solution approach. Deliverables: problem context document, initial constraints list, high-level integration map. No detailed design.

Alpha: Architecture is validated through prototyping. The team builds prototypes to test the riskiest architectural hypotheses. Does the proposed integration pattern actually work? Can the chosen technology stack handle the expected load? Is the authentication approach feasible? Alpha is the time to discover that your architectural assumptions were wrong — it is much cheaper to find out now than in beta. Deliverables: validated architecture approach, initial ADRs for key decisions, architecture brief for beta.

Beta: Architecture is implemented and refined. The team builds the real service based on the validated architecture. Detailed decisions emerge through delivery. The architect maintains the runway, participates in sprint ceremonies, and ensures the architecture remains coherent as the service grows. The solution architecture document evolves to reflect what is actually built (not what was initially imagined). Deliverables: living solution architecture document, complete ADR set, operational architecture.

Live: Architecture is operational and evolving. The focus shifts from building to running and improving. The architect ensures changes maintain architectural integrity, monitors for technical debt accumulation, and plans evolution in response to changing requirements. Deliverables: updated architecture documentation reflecting live system, technical debt register, evolution roadmap.

Service assessments happen at the end of alpha and beta phases. The architect must demonstrate: good decision-making (ADRs with honest options and trade-offs), standards alignment (TCoP, Service Standard), security by design (threat model, security architecture), and operational readiness (monitoring, DR, support model). These are the outputs of continuous architecture throughout delivery — not separate documentation exercises.

workedExample.title: Embedding Architecture in an Agile Delivery Team at DESNZ
workedExample.context: A new DESNZ digital service for managing energy efficiency grant applications is entering beta. The alpha validated the core approach: GOV.UK Forms for simple initial applications, a bespoke assessment workflow for caseworkers, integration with GOV.UK Pay for disbursement, and GOV.UK Notify for all communications. The beta team has 6 developers, a product owner, a delivery manager, and the Solution Architect. The team works in two-week sprints. The service must be ready for live assessment in 6 months.
workedExample.approach:
The Solution Architect establishes a working pattern that integrates architecture into the team's agile delivery.

Up-front (Week 1): The architect produces a concise beta architecture brief — 3 pages covering: system context (what the service integrates with), key architectural decisions from alpha (captured as ADRs), non-functional requirements (performance targets, availability targets, security classification), and the deployment architecture. This gives the team enough direction to start without waiting for a comprehensive design.

Ongoing runway (continuous): The architect works one sprint ahead. During sprint 1, while the team builds the application submission flow, the architect investigates the GOV.UK Pay integration for sprint 2 — confirming the API contract, resolving authentication questions, and writing the integration ADR. When the team reaches sprint 2, the architectural questions are already answered.

Sprint ceremonies: The architect attends refinement (identifying architectural implications of upcoming stories), sprint review (checking what was built aligns with the architecture), and is available on Slack for questions during sprints. They do not attend every stand-up but join when the team is working on architecturally significant components.

Design authority engagement: Every 4 weeks, the architect presents the service's architecture to the departmental design authority — not for approval (the team has authority to make decisions) but for peer review and awareness. This catches cross-cutting concerns ('did you know another team is building a similar workflow engine?') and provides feedback that improves quality.

Assessment preparation: In month 4, the architect begins preparing for the live service assessment — ensuring the solution architecture document reflects what was actually built, ADRs are complete and current, security evidence is documented, and operational readiness can be demonstrated. This is not a last-minute exercise — it is assembling evidence that has accumulated throughout delivery.
workedExample.outcome: The service passes its live assessment with strong feedback on architecture decision-making. The assessment panel specifically notes the quality of ADRs and the clear alignment between the architecture documentation and what was demonstrated. The team reports that architecture felt integrated into their work rather than imposed on it — the architect resolved blockers before they hit, and governance happened without ceremony.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The architect's most valuable contribution was not designing things but removing uncertainty. By working one sprint ahead, they ensured the team never had to stop and wait for an architectural decision. The brief up-front design gave enough structure without constraining the team. The regular design authority engagement caught one significant issue (a reuse opportunity with another team's workflow engine) that saved 3 sprints of work.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Architect Who Blocked Delivery
civilServiceScenario.background: A digital service team has been in beta for 4 months. The delivery manager has raised a concern with the programme board: the Solution Architect is blocking delivery. Specifically: the architect requires all API designs to be reviewed and approved before development begins (adding 3-5 days to each story), insists on comprehensive architecture documentation for every component (which the team considers unnecessary for simple CRUD operations), and has rejected a team decision to use a specific library because it is not on the departmental approved list (even though the approved alternatives are inferior for the use case). The team's velocity has dropped 30% since the architect joined. The delivery manager has asked the programme board to remove the architect from the team.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You are a senior architect asked to mediate. You must assess whether the architect's concerns are valid (some may be), help them adjust their approach to enable rather than block delivery, and rebuild the relationship between the architect and the delivery team.
constraints: The architect has genuine concerns about API quality and technology governance
The team has genuine frustration about being slowed down
The service assessment is in 2 months and the team is behind schedule
Some of the architect's previous reviews have caught genuine quality issues
The library dispute involves a security consideration that the team may not appreciate
The delivery manager and architect have a poor working relationship
The programme board wants a resolution within 2 weeks
Removing the architect entirely would leave no architectural oversight
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Lead Architect mediating between the embedded architect and the delivery team.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This is a common scenario that occurs when architects apply governance-heavy practices in agile environments. The architect's instincts (quality, security, consistency) are right — but their methods (approval gates, comprehensive documentation, blanket rejections) are wrong for the context.

The mediation should: validate the architect's concerns (API quality matters, security matters), challenge their methods (review does not need to block progress — review after implementation catches the same issues without delaying delivery), propose alternative patterns (pair programming on architecturally significant stories, lightweight review criteria with only blocking concerns requiring pre-approval, ADRs only for significant decisions not every component), and address the library dispute specifically (if there is a genuine security concern, articulate it clearly so the team can make an informed decision rather than simply being told 'no').

The relationship repair requires the architect to demonstrate value (catching genuine issues, providing helpful guidance) without imposing cost (delays, bureaucracy). Quick wins: approve the library with a documented rationale for the exception, reduce documentation requirements to ADRs only for significant decisions, and move to post-implementation review for most API designs with pre-review only for external-facing APIs.

practiceArtefact.type: Architecture Engagement Model for Agile Delivery
practiceArtefact.description: Design an architecture engagement model for a team of 8 developers working in two-week sprints on a government digital service. The model should specify: what architecture work happens before sprints begin (up-front), what happens during sprints (ongoing), what governance touch-points exist, what documentation is produced and when, and how the architect stays ahead of delivery without blocking it.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Be specific about when the architect participates in which ceremonies, what the threshold is for an architecture decision requiring an ADR versus team autonomy, how the architecture runway is maintained, and what happens when the team encounters an unexpected architectural challenge mid-sprint. Consider the government context: service assessments require evidence, security teams need engagement, and governance bodies expect visibility.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Architecture Engagement Model: [Service Name]**

Team: 8 developers, 1 PO, 1 DM, 1 SA | Sprints: 2 weeks | Phase: Beta

**1. Up-Front (Once, at beta start):**
- Architecture brief (3 pages max): system context, key ADRs from alpha, NFRs, deployment architecture
- Security architecture with threat model (engagement with departmental security team)
- Integration contracts agreed with external system owners
- Observability strategy (what to monitor, what to alert on)

**2. Sprint-Ahead (Continuous — architect works 1-2 sprints ahead):**
- Weekly: review upcoming backlog, identify stories with architectural implications
- Investigate and resolve architectural questions before team reaches them
- Produce ADRs for decisions that affect system structure (target: 1-2 per sprint)
- Engage external teams (security, operations, other services) proactively

**3. During Sprints:**
- Refinement (every sprint): attend to explain architectural context for upcoming stories
- Available on Slack: respond to architectural questions within 2 hours
- Pair programming: join developers for architecturally significant stories (estimated 2-3 per sprint)
- Sprint review: attend to verify alignment and catch drift early

**4. Governance Touch-Points:**
- Design Authority: present every 4 weeks (peer review, not approval)
- Security review: formal review at sprint 6 and sprint 12 (pre-assessment)
- Architecture documentation: updated monthly (living document, not one-off)

**5. Decision Authority:**

| Decision Type | Who Decides | Documentation |
|---|---|---|
| Internal component design | Team | Code + tests |
| Library/tool selection (approved list) | Team | None required |
| Library/tool selection (not on approved list) | Team + SA discussion | Brief ADR |
| External API design | SA review before publication | ADR |
| Integration pattern | SA decides (with team input) | ADR |
| Security architecture change | SA + Security team | ADR + threat model update |
| Technology stack change | Design Authority | Full ADR with options |

**6. When Things Go Wrong (Mid-Sprint Architectural Surprise):**
- Team raises to SA immediately (Slack or huddle)
- SA assesses: can this be resolved within the sprint, or does it need more time?
- If resolvable: SA and developer pair to resolve, document decision as ADR
- If not resolvable: story is parked, moved to next sprint. SA resolves the architectural question in the current sprint so it is ready for the team next sprint.
- Never: team proceeds in a direction they know is architecturally wrong to 'keep velocity up'

reflectiveQuestions: How does architecture work in your current agile team? Is the architect embedded in the team or separate from it? How does that affect the relationship?
Have you experienced tension between architectural quality and delivery speed? How was it resolved — did quality or speed win, and what was the consequence?
What decisions in your current service were made up-front versus emerging during delivery? In hindsight, were they in the right category?
How do you maintain architectural coherence when a team is making rapid changes across multiple sprints? What signals tell you that the architecture is drifting?
Think about your last service assessment. Was the architecture evidence assembled during delivery or scrambled together at the last minute? What would you do differently?

knowledgeCheck.question: What does 'just-enough up-front design' mean in agile architecture?
options: Designing everything in detail before any code is written
Making the minimum foundational decisions needed for delivery to begin, deferring everything that can wait
Not doing any design at all and letting everything emerge
Producing a comprehensive solution architecture document before alpha
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Just-enough up-front design means making foundational decisions (hosting, security architecture, integration approach, key technology choices) that are expensive to reverse, while deliberately deferring decisions that can be made later with more information. It provides enough structure for delivery to begin without constraining decisions that should emerge.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the architecture runway?
options: The total budget allocated to architecture work
Prepared architectural direction that stays one or two sprints ahead of what the team is building
The time between architecture design and system deployment
A document listing all future architecture decisions
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The architecture runway means the architect works slightly ahead of the delivery team — resolving architectural questions and making decisions before the team reaches them. This ensures delivery is never blocked waiting for architectural direction, while avoiding designing too far ahead of implementation.

knowledgeCheck.question: In which GDS delivery phase should the riskiest architectural hypotheses be validated?
options: Discovery — before any code is written
Alpha — through prototyping and technical spikes
Beta — through building the production service
Live — through monitoring production behaviour
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Alpha is specifically designed for validating risky hypotheses through prototyping. Testing whether your architectural approach works (integration patterns, technology choices, scalability assumptions) is much cheaper in alpha than discovering problems in beta when you are building the production system.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most common cause of architects blocking agile delivery?
options: Making too few architectural decisions
Applying governance-heavy approval processes that add delays to every story
Being too available to the team for questions
Documenting decisions too quickly
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Architects block delivery when they require pre-approval for decisions that the team could make themselves, mandate comprehensive documentation for simple components, or operate as a gate rather than a guide. The fix is proportionate governance: pre-review only for significant or irreversible decisions, team autonomy for everything else.

knowledgeCheck.question: What should be intentional (designed up-front) versus emergent (evolving during delivery)?
options: Everything should be designed up-front for government services due to compliance requirements
Everything should emerge because agile means no planning
System boundaries and security architecture should be intentional; internal component design should emerge
Only database schemas need up-front design; everything else emerges
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Intentional architecture covers decisions that affect the system's boundaries and interaction with the outside world (APIs, integrations, security, data flows) — these are expensive to change and affect other teams. Internal component design, detailed data models, and implementation patterns should emerge through delivery as the team learns about the problem.
